description: We are a team passionate about space, technology, and problem-solving. We enjoy coding, data analysis, and design, and we want to build a creative, data-driven solution using NASA's open data while learning and having fun along the way.
summary: Karacadağ, a basaltic shield volcano in southeastern Türkiye, has to our knowledge never been examined as a planetary analog. BlackMountain is a bilingual web application that evaluates it against lunar and Martian targets, pairing open NASA and partner-agency data with our own field survey. Among eight selected terrestrial sites compared with a single terrain metric, including seven previously studied analog sites, Karacadağ ranks third in similarity to the lunar mare around the Mare Tranquillitatis pit, ahead of Haughton Crater and the Atacama Desert. Against Arsia Mons on Mars it scores equal to Askja in Iceland, where Apollo astronauts trained. Using our ten-oxide similarity metric, its lava matches basalt analysed by the Spirit rover at Gusev crater more closely than Martian and lunar basalts match each other. On 14 November 2026 our team scanned in 3D a partially roofed collapse pit roughly 11 m wide and 5.7 m deep. Each score is shown beside the point where the analogy fails, presenting Karacadağ as an accessible, low-cost potential test site for rover mobility and pit-access operations ahead of missions to the Moon and Mars.
details:
Measuring an unstudied volcano in Türkiye with the same ruler as the Moon and Mars.

What it does and how it works

The challenge asks for new Earth locations that analog the permanent Moon base sites and Mars, judged by more than visual similarity. BlackMountain answers with Karacadağ, a basaltic shield volcano in southeastern Türkiye that, to our knowledge, has never been studied as a planetary analog. Our web application compares it with three exploration targets, Arsia Mons on Mars, the Mare Tranquillitatis pit region and the Shackleton connecting ridge at the lunar south pole, using real satellite data, published rock analyses and our own field work. It also ranks Karacadağ against seven analog sites already in use, and every score is shown with the point where the analogy breaks. Measured with one method, it ranks third of eight sites for the lunar maria, and its lava is chemically closer to Martian basalt than Martian and lunar basalts are to each other.

Every elevation model, whether from Earth, the Moon or Mars, is resampled to the same 62 by 62 km window on a common grid of about 121 m. Slope and roughness are measured over a 480 m baseline, coarser than any input model, so that no dataset benefits from its own resolution. Their distributions are compared with the Jensen-Shannon distance and combined with relief into a terrain match score. Shadow is traced with planetary curvature at seven sun elevations, and rock chemistry is compared across ten major oxides.

Under this model, Karacadağ matched the Tranquillitatis mare at 63 out of 100, third of eight sites and ahead of Mauna Loa, Atacama, Haughton Crater, the San Francisco Volcanic Field and Death Valley. Against Arsia Mons it scored 60, sixth of eight but level with Askja and above Haughton Crater and Craters of the Moon, and against the Shackleton ridge it scored 46, also sixth. Mauna Loa, the established Martian shield volcano analog, ranked first for Mars, which we use as a sanity check on the method. Under our ten-oxide similarity metric, Ovabağ lava, from the youngest part of the volcano, scored 65 against basalt analysed by the Spirit rover at Gusev crater, while the Martian and lunar reference basalts score only 56 against each other.

On 14 November 2026 we surveyed the Ovabağ lava field and scanned a collapse pit that orbit cannot see, since it is smaller than one pixel of the 30 m elevation data we used for Karacadağ. The smartphone scan of 3.1 million points gives preliminary dimensions of an opening of 12.7 by 11.7 m and a depth of 5.7 m, with about a third of the pit still roofed. At about 15:00 the pit was 2.7 °C warmer than the air above it. A single reading does not establish thermal buffering, the property that makes lunar pits candidate shelters, but it motivates further investigation.

Benefits

BlackMountain is useful to several groups. Teams planning rover, instrument and crew tests can see what Karacadağ can rehearse, such as terrain, rock chemistry and pit geometry, and what it cannot, such as polar light and the lunar thermal environment. For planetary scientists, Karacadağ is reachable by road near Diyarbakır and exposes young, sparsely vegetated basalt with lava tubes and collapsed roofs, which makes it a candidate low-cost test site compared with remote analogs such as Atacama, Haughton Crater or Iceland. Students and educators get an interactive way to compare Earth, the Moon and Mars through measurements rather than impressions. Because every site is measured with the same procedure, the comparison can also be repeated for other candidate locations.

Intended impact

We aim to add Karacadağ to the set of terrestrial analogs on evidence that anyone can check, and to show that analog selection can be a transparent comparison rather than a judgment by eye. Earth cannot reproduce lunar or Martian gravity, vacuum or radiation, and light similarity with the Shackleton ridge is only 18 out of 100, so the application states these limits next to the scores. We also hope the project opens planetary analog research to students and researchers in southeastern Türkiye.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Web application. TypeScript, React, Vite and Tailwind CSS, with three.js (react-three-fiber, drei) for the 3D terrain, Recharts for charts, Zustand for state and Framer Motion for transitions.
  • Architecture. A static site with no server. The browser computes the terrain and light scores from the data grids when the page loads.
  • Data pipeline. Python with rasterio and numpy fetches the open data and writes each layer as a 512 by 512 floating-point grid with a manifest of its source and resolution. The terrain results were reproduced independently in Python.
  • Data. NASA (SRTM, VIIRS through GIBS, LRO LOLA, MOLA, the Planetary Data System and the Lunar Sample Compendium), ESA (Sentinel-1 and Mars Express HRSC), USGS, and published Karacadağ rock analyses (Agostini et al. 2022).
  • Hardware. A smartphone for the 3D scan of the pit and a handheld temperature and humidity sensor.

Creativity

Most analog studies start from a well-known site. We started from a volcano that had not been considered as an analog, measured it with the same ruler as the Moon, Mars and the sites NASA already uses, and then added field evidence that orbit cannot see. In the bilingual Turkish and English application, the space bar morphs Karacadağ into Mars or the Moon at the same scale, and each of the eleven chapters is labelled as field measurement, orbital data, published analysis or illustrative material.

Factors we considered

Our main concern was that a new site should earn its place on evidence rather than enthusiasm. We used a common baseline so that sensor resolution could not bias the ranking, included established analogs as a reference, and stated where our samples differ from the targets, since the Martian chemistry comes from Gusev crater rather than Arsia Mons. The rankings depend on window position and weighting, so a sensitivity analysis is our next step, together with a season-long temperature logger in the pit, a tape and GPS check of the scan, and the same search over other volcanic fields.
